question: In astronomy, what are so dense that not even light can escape their gravity?

question: In our bodies, the chest cavity is a clear example of a system at what?

question: What useful tool helps scientists work with, understand and make predictions about extremely complex systems?
gold_core_evidence_sets: [[{"span_id":"openstax-cp2e-a052d9fae2a90e13_pv1.3.2_ch01_p0031_b004_gold_candidate","document_id":"openstax-cp2e-a052d9fae2a90e13","chapter_id":"1","char_start":17811,"char_end":18570,"verbatim_text":"A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult (or impossible) to display directly. While a model is justified with experimental proof, it is only accurate under limited situations. An example is the planetary model of the atom in which electrons are pictured as orbiting the nucleus, analogous to the way planets orbit the Sun. (See Figure 1.10.) We cannot observe electron orbits directly, but the mental image helps explain the observations we can make, such as the emission of light from hot gases (atomic spectra). Physicists use models for a variety of purposes. Because humans live under such circumstances, classical physics seems intuitively reasonable, while many aspects of modern physics seem bizarre. This is why models are so useful in modern physics—they let us conceptualize phenomena we do not ordinarily experience. source: {"dataset":"SciQ standardized","source_question_id":"sciq-test-00432","support":"One important phenomenon related to the relative strength of cohesive and adhesive forces is capillary action—the tendency of a fluid to be raised or suppressed in a narrow tube, or capillary tube. Capillary Action The tendency of a fluid to be raised or suppressed in a narrow tube, or capillary tube, is called capillary action. If a capillary tube is placed vertically into a liquid, as shown in Figure 11.34, capillary action will raise or suppress the liquid inside the tube depending on the combination of substances. When the switch is closed, a magnetic field is produced in the coil on the top part of the iron ring and transmitted to the coil on the bottom part of the ring. The galvanometer is used to detect any current induced in the coil on the bottom. It was found that each time the switch is closed, the galvanometer detects a current in one direction in the coil on the bottom. (You can also observe this in a physics lab.) Each time the switch is opened, the galvanometer detects a current in the opposite direction. Interestingly, if the switch remains closed or open for any length of time, there is no current through the galvanometer. Closing and opening the switch induces the current. It is the change in magnetic field that creates the current. More basic than the current that flows is the emf that causes it. question: What is the term for the use of radioactive decay to estimate the ages of fossils and rock?
gold_core_evidence_sets: [[{"span_id":"openstax-physics-a3f75487411ef13d_pv1.3.2_ch22_p0780_b004_gold_candidate","document_id":"openstax-physics-a3f75487411ef13d","chapter_id":"22","char_start":74436,"char_end":75927,"verbatim_text":"Radioactive dating or radiometric dating is a clever use of naturally occurring radioactivity. Its most familiar application is carbon-14 dating. Carbon-14 is an isotope of carbon that is produced when solar neutrinos strike [EQUATION: to the 14th power N] particles within the atmosphere. Radioactive carbon has the same chemistry as stable carbon, and so it mixes into the biosphere, where it is consumed and becomes part of every living organism. Carbon-14 has an abundance of 1.3 parts per trillion of normal carbon, so if you know the number of carbon nuclei in an object (perhaps determined by mass and Avogadro’s number), you can multiply that number by [EQUATION: 1.3 × 10 to the − 12 power] to find the number of [EQUATION: to the 14th power C] nuclei within the object. Over time, carbon-14 will naturally decay back to [EQUATION: to the 14th power N] with a half-life of 5,730 years (note that this is an example of beta decay). When an organism dies, carbon exchange with the environment ceases, and [EQUATION: to the 14th power C] is not replenished. By comparing the abundance of [EQUATION: to the 14th power C] in an artifact, such as mummy wrappings, with the normal abundance in living tissue, it is possible to determine the artifact’s age (or time since death).
